\chapter{Numbers 11–20 and Weather}
\label{ch:ml-numbers-and-weather}

\section[\ml{പതിനൊന്ന്} — \ml{ഇരുപത്}]{\ml{പതിനൊന്ന്}, \ml{ഇരുപത്} — transparent \textquotedblleft{}two-tens,\textquotedblright{} matching Tamil closely}

\label{lesson:ML-C20-pathinonnu-irupathu}



\begin{quote}
Malayalam keeps the same \textquotedblleft{}two-tens\textquotedblright{} idea you've now seen across this whole family — and here it's still fully visible on the surface, almost identically to its closest cousin, Tamil.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
Malayalam's teens echo \textbf{\ml{പത്ത്}} (\emph{pathu}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{ten}\textquotedblright{}) plus each digit. \textbf{\ml{പതിനൊന്ന്}} (\emph{pathinonnu}) is 11, \textbf{\ml{പന്ത്രണ്ട്}} (\emph{panthraṇṭŭ}) is 12, and the pattern continues through \textbf{\ml{പത്തൊമ്പത്}} (\emph{pathompathu}, 19) — the same digit-plus-ten-echo compounding as its Dravidian cousins.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{ഇരുപത്}} (\emph{irupathu}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{twenty}\textquotedblright{}) = \textbf{\ml{ഇരു}} (\emph{iru}, an older word for \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{two}\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\ml{പത്ത്}} (\emph{pathu}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{ten}\textquotedblright{}) — still fully visible as \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{two-tens}\textquotedblright{} today. This matches \textbf{Tamil's own} \emph{irupathu} almost letter-for-letter, both languages having kept this compound transparent — unlike Telugu's \emph{iravai}, which most likely continues the same underlying pattern but has worn down past the point of visibly splitting apart.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pathinonnu, panthraṇṭŭ\textquotedblright{} — 11, 12
  \item \textquotedblleft{}iru\textquotedblright{} — an older word for two, \textquotedblleft{}pathu\textquotedblright{} — ten
  \item \textquotedblleft{}irupathu\textquotedblright{} — twenty, \textquotedblleft{}two-tens,\textquotedblright{} transparent
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How are Malayalam's teens built? (\textbf{\ml{പത്ത്}} (ten) + a digit, compounded.) What two pieces build \textbf{\ml{ഇരുപത്}} (twenty)? (\textbf{\ml{ഇരു}} \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{} + \textbf{\ml{പത്ത്}} \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{two-tens}.\textquotedblright{}) Which other Dravidian language keeps this exact same transparent compound for twenty? (\textbf{Tamil}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ml{കാലാവസ്ഥ}]{\ml{കാലാവസ്ഥ} — \textquotedblleft{}the state of time,\textquotedblright{} an echo of Spanish's tiempo}

\label{lesson:ML-C20-kalavastha}



\begin{quote}
Remember Spanish's \emph{tiempo}, one word for both \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}weather\textquotedblright{}? Malayalam reaches the same connection between time and weather — but builds it as a compound instead of reusing one word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{കാലാവസ്ഥ}} (\emph{kālāvastha}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{weather}\textquotedblright{} — built from:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{കാലം}} (\emph{kālam}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{time}\textquotedblright{}) — Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{काल}} (\emph{kāla}), \textquotedblleft{}time,\textquotedblright{} also the name of the god \textbf{Kāla} (an epithet of Śiva/Yama as the personification of time).
  \item \textbf{\ml{അവസ്ഥ}} (\emph{avastha}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{state, condition}\textquotedblright{}) — Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{अवस्था}} (\emph{avasthā}).
\end{itemize}

So \emph{kālāvastha} literally means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the state of time}\textquotedblright{} — a genuinely different construction than Spanish's \emph{tiempo}, but reaching for the exact same underlying idea: weather as bound up with time. Where Spanish just \textbf{reuses} its word for \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} to also mean \textquotedblleft{}weather,\textquotedblright{} Malayalam \textbf{compounds} \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} with \textquotedblleft{}state\textquotedblright{} to build a brand-new word for the same concept.

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{മഴ} \ml{പെയ്യുന്നു}.} — \textquotedblleft{}It's raining.\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{rain is falling}.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{mazha peyyunnu.})
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kālāvastha\textquotedblright{} — weather, \textquotedblleft{}the state of time\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kālam\textquotedblright{} — time, \textquotedblleft{}avastha\textquotedblright{} — state
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mazha peyyunnu\textquotedblright{} — it's raining, \textquotedblleft{}rain is falling\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two Sanskrit pieces of \textbf{\ml{കാലാവസ്ഥ}}, and what does the whole word literally mean? (\textbf{\ml{കാലം}}, \textquotedblleft{}time,\textquotedblright{} + \textbf{\ml{അവസ്ഥ}}, \textquotedblleft{}state\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the state of time}.\textquotedblright{}) What earlier lesson does this echo, and how is the construction different? (\textbf{Spanish's \emph{tiempo}} — Spanish reuses ONE word for both senses; Malayalam \textbf{compounds} two separate words instead.) What word does Malayalam use for \textquotedblleft{}rain\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\ml{മഴ}}, \emph{mazha}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
